title: Ezekiel 28:20–26
context: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet with a message against Sidon, the Phoenician city to the north of Tyre (28:20–21). The LORD is against Sidon and will be glorified and shown holy in her through judgments of pestilence and sword, so that “they will know that I am the LORD” (28:22–23). The oracles against Israel’s neighbors then close with a word for Israel: there will no longer be a pricking brier or a hurting thorn from the surrounding peoples who scorned them (28:24). When the LORD gathers the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, they will dwell securely in the land he gave to his servant Jacob, building houses and planting vineyards, and they will know that he is the LORD their God (28:25–26). Readers differ on how this promise is fulfilled: in the return from Babylon (compare Ezra 1:1–4), in a future restoration of Israel, in Christ and his people, or in some combination of these. These views run across both traditions. Both read the passage as shared ground: the LORD’s judgments on the nations serve the purpose that he be known, and his faithfulness to his scattered people outlasts their exile.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to the prophet again, and the last oracle in this series against Israel’s neighbors concerns Sidon. Arminian readers see the LORD’s word reaching each surrounding people in turn, every one accountable for how it has treated others and for its posture toward him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as marking the LORD’s sovereign word over yet another nation, completing a circle of oracles around Israel that began in chapter 25. Shared ground: both traditions read the brief Sidon oracle as closely tied to the Tyre oracles before it, since the two Phoenician cities were neighbors and often named together (compare Jeremiah 47:4; Joel 3:4).

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against it,
verses.arminianNotes: “Son of man, set your face toward Sidon, and prophesy against it.” Setting the face is a recurring prophetic gesture in Ezekiel (compare 6:2; 25:2). Arminian readers see the prophet’s posture as a sign of the LORD’s settled opposition to a people that had set itself against him and his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in the command the prophet’s role as a faithful messenger, speaking against a nation he may never visit, because the word is the LORD’s. Shared ground: both traditions read the title “son of man” as marking the prophet’s human standing as he carries the LORD’s word, and both see the gesture as a formal announcement of judgment.

verses.text: and say, ‘The Lord GOD says: “Behold, I am against you, Sidon. I will be glorified among you. Then they will know that I am the LORD, when I have executed judgments in her, and am sanctified in her.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD declares, “Behold, I am against you, Sidon. I will be glorified among you.” His judgments will show him holy. Arminian readers see the LORD’s glory revealed in just judgment that answers Sidon’s conduct, and they hear “they will know that I am the LORD” as a summons for the nations to recognize him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the LORD’s glory as the ultimate purpose of his acts in history, displayed in judgment as well as in mercy (compare Exodus 14:4). Shared ground: both traditions read the recurring phrase about knowing the LORD as central to Ezekiel’s message, and both see the LORD showing himself holy through righteous judgment, not arbitrary power.

verses.text: For I will send pestilence into her, and blood into her streets. The wounded will fall within her, with the sword on her on every side. Then they will know that I am the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will send pestilence into Sidon and blood into her streets, and the wounded will fall by the sword on every side. Arminian readers read these familiar instruments of judgment (compare 5:17; 14:19–21) soberly, as consequences falling on a city that had persisted in hostility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see pestilence and sword as means the LORD governs in executing justice, and they hear the refrain “Then they will know that I am the LORD” as the purpose of the judgment. Shared ground: both traditions treat the language of war and plague without elaboration, and both hold that the LORD judges justly and takes no pleasure in death (compare 18:23, 32).

verses.text: “ ‘ “There will no longer be a pricking brier to the house of Israel, nor a hurting thorn of any that are around them that scorned them. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes: “There will no longer be a pricking brier to the house of Israel, nor a hurting thorn of any that are around them that scorned them.” The image recalls the warning that peoples left in the land would be thorns (compare Numbers 33:55). Arminian readers see the LORD’s judgments as relief for a people long harassed by its neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as revealing a purpose behind the oracles against the nations: the LORD acts for the sake of his covenant people. Shared ground: both traditions read the brier and thorn as images of hostility and contempt, and both see the refrain, “Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD,” pointing beyond Israel’s relief to the knowledge of God.

verses.text: “ ‘The Lord GOD says: “When I have gathered the house of Israel from the peoples among whom they are scattered, and am shown as holy among them in the sight of the nations, then they will dwell in their own land which I gave to my servant Jacob.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises that when he has gathered the house of Israel and is shown holy among them, “they will dwell in their own land which I gave to my servant Jacob.” Arminian readers see the LORD’s faithfulness to his promise despite Israel’s unfaithfulness, offered to a people called to respond to him in trust and obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the gathering as the LORD’s sovereign work to vindicate his holy name before the nations (compare 36:22–24), resting on his promise to the patriarchs. Shared ground: both traditions root the gathering in the LORD’s promise to Jacob, and readers in both differ on whether it is fulfilled in the return from exile, a future restoration of Israel, Christ and his people, or a combination.

verses.text: They will dwell in it securely. Yes, they will build houses, plant vineyards, and will dwell securely when I have executed judgments on all those around them who have treated them with contempt. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “They will dwell in it securely. Yes, they will build houses, plant vineyards.” Arminian readers see a picture of settled peace (compare Jeremiah 29:5; Amos 9:14), the reversal of exile’s losses, and they hear the closing words, “they will know that I am the LORD their God,” as a restored covenant relationship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the security as the fruit of the LORD’s judgments on Israel’s enemies and of his covenant faithfulness, and they read “the LORD their God” as covenant language at its heart. Shared ground: both traditions read the promise soberly, without speculation about dates, and both see the LORD as the source of his people’s security, whatever view of its fulfillment readers hold.
